sections.title: Connecting the two halves

blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: Your PDFs do not cover this topic, so this page was written for the site. Your 12-week plan lists React, hooks, rendering, performance, state management and TypeScript. Check it against the official documentation, or give me a PDF to replace it.

blocks: This page ties React to the Spring Boot API from your guides: routing, calling the API, CORS, JWT handling and forms.

blocks.title: A full-stack request
blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser (React)
  participant S as Spring Boot API
  participant D as Database
  B->>S: POST /api/auth/login (email, password)
  S->>D: find user, check password hash
  S-->>B: access token, refresh token in HttpOnly cookie
  B->>S: GET /api/books with Authorization Bearer token
  S->>S: security filter chain validates the token
  S->>D: query
  S-->>B: 200 with JSON
  B->>B: setState, React re-renders

blocks.title: React Router
Gotcha
blocks.text: Hiding a route in React is not security: anyone can call your API directly. Authorisation must be enforced in Spring. Also, when Spring serves the built app, unknown paths like `/books/7` must return `index.html`, or a page refresh gives a 404.

sections.title: An API client
blocks: Put HTTP in one place, so the token, error handling and base URL are not repeated in every component.

sections.title: CORS, and why you often avoid it
blocks: The browser blocks JavaScript from reading responses from a different origin unless the server allows it. CORS is enforced by the browser: `curl` and Postman ignore it.

blocks.title: Spring: enable with http.cors(withDefaults())

blocks: In development, skip CORS with a Vite proxy, so the browser sees a single origin:

sections.title: Forms and validation errors
blocks: Show Spring's validation errors next to the fields. Client checks give fast feedback; the server has the final word.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: **Your React app gets a CORS error from Spring. Walk through it.** The browser sends a preflight `OPTIONS` for non-simple requests, and the response must allow the origin, method and headers. With Spring Security, enable `http.cors(...)` so the preflight is handled before authentication; otherwise it gets a 401. In development, a Vite proxy avoids the issue.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Security lives in Spring; hiding UI is only cosmetic.
- Keep HTTP in one API client.
- CORS is enforced by the browser.
- Choose token storage knowing the XSS and CSRF trade-offs.
- Serve `index.html` for unknown paths so client routes survive a refresh.

items.question: Why does a request work in Postman but fail with CORS in the browser?
items.answer: CORS is enforced by browsers only. Postman does not apply the same-origin policy.

items.question: Why does `/books/7` give a 404 on refresh in production?
items.answer: The server looks for that path and finds nothing. It must fall back to `index.html` so the client router can handle it.

items.question: Is a `RequireAuth` route enough to protect admin data?
items.answer: No. It only hides the screen. The API must check authorisation on every request.

items.question: What is the XSS risk of `localStorage` for tokens?
items.answer: Any script running on your page, including an injected one, can read and send the token.
